### Gap scan: jvmcontract gaps names what the tool's own checker approximates, and every B9/B11 example records what strict mode would cost it

change `ympzqxkvvswo` · [log `3beb15f8028e`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/7cacdb56-4c74-4880-a06e-f98031283c0f/3beb15f8028ef10402453f4b9ff856254a9ddc5ae7d864978cde99959286ea5e.jsonl.gz)

Step 1a of llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md. lib/src/bmc/gaps.rs walks the bytecode a proof's roots may reach, resolving calls as the engine does, and names each construct the engine approximates rather than implements as a gap with a stable id (kind and member, @jdk-&lt;version> for a JDK call): a skipped JDK constructor, a void or reference-returning JDK instance method, a monitor (no null check), a field hidden by a subclass, a literal compared by reference, a class initializer the engine never runs, an object converted inside a string concatenation. It also lists the JDK calls the engine reproduces exactly and relies on, and what it already refuses. The new command is `jvmcontract gaps --classes DIR --target C#m [--json]`. bmc::models_jdk_static gives the scan the engine's list of modelled static JDK methods. `build.py --scan-gaps` compiles each B9/B11 example on a javac app, scans both versions of a regression proof, and replaces the example's 'Gap scan (...)' note.

Result over the 56 examples scanned: strict mode moves no recorded verdict. 54 meet no gap. 013 and 071 (Quorum's vote rule, proved by JBMC) meet four enum class initializers and a literal compared by reference, but the native engine already refuses both, since enum constants are static fields that aren't compile-time constants. Not scanned: Box Office's 006-008 (its Gradle verifier), the real-world 105-109 (no classes in the repository), and the approaches that are not proofs over bytecode.

Correction to the brief: step 1b's allow-list of exact JDK calls ('Object.&lt;init>, and calls already covered by lib/models') is too narrow. The scan shows 14 examples relying on Record.&lt;init>() and 25 on the JDK exceptions' (), (String) and (String, Throwable) constructors. These change nothing a proof observes and throw nothing, so they belong on the list; gaps::exact_jdk_call is that list. Also, the string-conversion gap only arises in bytecode from javac 9-18: from JDK 19, javac calls String.valueOf first, which the engine refuses.

Verified with a new integration test (both review reproducers, a void JDK mutator of an argument array via Random.nextBytes, field hiding, literal identity, a class initializer and the exact calls, each by id) and GapScanTest in test_build.py (133 tests). The full lib suite passes (118 unit, 51 integration tests). `build.py --render-only` reports no page stale; the notes are not part of any claim.

### Identity and initialization: a hidden field is a second field and a literal one object, as on the JVM, and a class initializer the tool's own checker does not run is a named gap

change `uvwzvlqwooqx` · [log `115839ac3ae9`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/7cacdb56-4c74-4880-a06e-f98031283c0f/115839ac3ae9f7847dbb12a27088c8b12d678a0aedf35999997eb18ecf78686f.jsonl.gz)

Step 1c of llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md. Fields are now resolved by the JVM's field lookup (JVMS 5.4.3.2, ClassPath::resolve_field). A field that a subclass declares again is kept as a second field under its declaring class's name (ClassPath::field_key), in both the tool's own checker and the interpreter that replays its witnesses. The interpreter had the same name-only keying, so it confirmed the engine's wrong witness. Each path of the checker keeps one object per distinct string or class literal, as the JVM interns them. A string concatenation stays a new object, as JLS 15.18.1 says; this was checked on JDK 25.

A class whose initialization runs an application &lt;clinit> is a class-initializer gap. gaps::initializers lists those initializers in JVMS 5.5 order: superclasses first, then superinterfaces with default methods, then the class itself. The engine meets the gap at a path's first new, getstatic or invokestatic of the class, and the static scan uses the same function. Under --gaps strict the path is refused by name; under --gaps assume the initializer is taken to have run and thrown nothing, and the verdict names it. --engine auto now asks JBMC when every gap the checker refused is a class initializer, because JBMC runs initializers; JDK-call gaps still don't fall back. Because hidden fields and literal identity are now implemented, they are no longer gap kinds (the result schema and docs follow).

Verified by the new integration test identity_and_initialization_agree_with_the_jvm, which runs every claim on a real JVM first. On the parent commit's binary, four claims the JVM refutes came back Verified: hiding 'result == 2', sameLiteral '!result', sameClass '!result', and boom 'result == n', which throws ExceptionInInitializerError on the JVM. Now the first three are violations that the interpreter replays. boom is refused by name under strict and Verified-with-assumption under assume, and JBMC gives a violation (ExceptionInInitializerError) for it under auto; a harmless initializer is refused under strict too. cargo test --release passes (119 unit, 53 integration tests), and so do build.py's 136 tests. build.py --scan-gaps rescanned all 56 B9/B11 examples in 41 s. Only 013's and 071's notes changed (their literal-identity gap is gone, their four enum initializers stay), so strict mode still moves no recorded verdict and no verification job is needed.

### Conformance corpus: 93 claims about 54 small methods, each held to a real JVM, and no Verified the JVM refutes from the tool's own checker under strict (verification pending)

change `syquyqqkprxu` · [log `e970a900beb3`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/7cacdb56-4c74-4880-a06e-f98031283c0f/e970a900beb3a9a033aa8ba055118573acb9b3c26f118dd7445b129249c63787.jsonl.gz)

Step 1d of llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md. lib/tests/conformance.rs runs a corpus of small Java methods (lib/tests/conformance/conformance/Conformance.java). The cases cover the gap reproducers of steps 1b and 1c, JDK constructors given a negative capacity, exceptions (finally over a return, nested handlers, bounds, casts, throw null, rethrow), aliasing, null arrays, record constructors, dispatch, and arithmetic edge cases (MIN_VALUE / -1 in both widths, negative remainders, shift counts of 32, 33, 64 and -1, narrowing, overflow). The JVM is the reference. A Java runner (lib/tests/conformance/Runner.java) runs every call, and every claim's generated property harness, each in a class loader of its own. So whether a claim is refuted is the JVM's answer on the harness, and every witness an engine reports is run on the JVM as well.

Inline, in 11 s, the corpus checks the tool's own checker under --gaps strict and assume, and the interpreter against the JVM call by call. Of the 93 claims, 48 are refuted on the JVM. None of them is Verified under strict, and every violation's witness refutes the harness on the JVM. Under assume a refuted claim is Verified only with its gap named. The native verdict is recorded for each claim, so coverage changes show up too.

The corpus found a bug in the interpreter, which replays every witness and executes the behavioural contracts (B8). new ArrayList&lt;>(n), new HashMap&lt;>(n), new HashSet&lt;>(n), new HashMap&lt;>(4, f) and new StringBuilder(n) returned normally there for a negative capacity (or a load factor of 0 or less), where the JVM throws IllegalArgumentException or NegativeArraySizeException. The test failed on capacity(-1) before the fix, which makes lib/src/interp/natives.rs throw what the JVM does. This is the brief's point that the engines and the interpreter share semantics, so their agreement proves nothing about the JVM.

A null array parameter, or one array passed as two parameters, is outside the domain both engines prove over (JBMC runs under --java-assume-inputs-non-null), but the domain line did not say so. It now reads 'a: int[] of length ≤ 8, not null', ending '; no two the same array' when there are two arrays or more (harness::domain, used by both regression and property proofs). The corpus has three such cases, and checks that a Verified for them states the restriction that leaves out the JVM's refuting input. Pages already recorded keep the old text until they are re-run; build.py's domain regexes still match.

The brief is out of date in one respect: it plans the JBMC side of the corpus as examples under a new false-success defect tag. A corpus is a table of claims over one class, and examples would put one claim on each page. So JBMC and --engine auto run the same corpus in an ignored test, the_corpus_agrees_with_the_jvm_under_jbmc_and_auto (cargo test --release --test conformance -- --ignored), queued as pipeline job 20261106-021741-conformance-corpus-under-jbmc-and-engine. The tag is not added. lib/README.md documents the corpus and the domain's wording.

### Confirming mode: --engine auto --confirm has JBMC prove again what the tool's own checker proved, and a disagreement is no verdict of either (verification pending)

change `nkyxuqqvnlyy` · [log `5665eed8c615`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/7cacdb56-4c74-4880-a06e-f98031283c0f/5665eed8c6152a598f8eef83a67e44c3dd67fd360123a743db2b7b28b7c94485.jsonl.gz)

Step 1e of llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md. Under --engine auto --confirm, for property and regression proofs, a statement the own checker proved goes to JBMC, which proves it again in one run over every input. That run uses the same harness and class path; the interval stages only find small witnesses sooner. The result's search.confirmation has a status (confirmed, disagreed, no-verdict, not-asked), the checker, its seconds and a reason, and a line under the ✓ says it in words. JBMC refuting the proof gives Unverifiable, 'the engines disagree' (finding engines-disagree), with JBMC's witness as the counterexample. The interpreter's run of the harness on that witness is shown but decides nothing, since it shares the own checker's models. A proof that assumed a JDK call under --gaps assume is not sent to JBMC, which would approximate the same call without naming it. An assumed class initializer is checked, since JBMC runs it. The option is opt-in, and the CLI refuses it under any engine but auto.

Departures from the brief: it says a disagreement is 'its own outcome, never either verdict'. Here that is Unverifiable plus the disagreed status, not a fourth Verdict, because every caller already treats Unverifiable as no verdict. > - An unresolved JDK constructor is skipped, a void JDK instance method does nothing, and one that returns a reference gets a fresh opaque object.

> &lt;/pasted_content id="d132">
>
> *… (shortened; the log has the full text)*

**Reply:**

Short answer: checking these properly costs very little at run time. What it costs is coverage: programs the engine accepts today would be refused. Your third option fits that well, provided the LLM proposes and the tool checks.

## What each fix costs at run time

| Gap | The proper fix | Run-time cost |
|---|---|---|
| A JDK constructor or method the engine doesn't model (skipped, a no-op, or a fresh opaque object) | Refuse it by name | **Lower.** The path stops early. |
| `synchronized` with no null check | One null check, then nothing (single-threaded) | One branch per monitor, which is rare |
| Fields looked up by name alone | Look the field up by its declaring class when the bytecode is read | Nothing during the proof |
| String and class literals as fresh objects | One object per distinct literal | Nothing to speak of |
| Static initializers never run | Refuse, or record an "already initialized" assumption | Nothing. Actually running them could be expensive, but neither option does. |
| JBMC's own stubs | Read its warnings, or one preflight run | Free, or a few seconds |
| **Having JBMC confirm a native `Verified`** | A second engine re-proves it | **Expensive.** On the recorded examples JBMC is often 10–100× slower: 141 took 2 s native against 101 s, and 142 ran JBMC out of memory. |

So "fully verify" isn't expensive because of the semantic fixes. Only the cross-engine confirmation is, and that's already optional in the draft (open question 2).

- **A disagreement is neither `Verified` nor `Violation`.** The result is `Unverifiable` with "the engines disagree", and JBMC's witness is the counterexample. The interpreter's run on that witness is shown but decides nothing, because it shares the own checker's models. The message asks for a JVM run to settle which engine is wrong.

- **The new gaps:** a JDK method returning a primitive (`jdk-primitive-method`, e.g. `Random.nextInt(bound)`), and a static JDK method the checker doesn't model (`jdk-static-method`, e.g. `Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros`).
- **No assume form:** the checker could only make the returned value up, so `--gaps assume` refuses them as strict does. The reason says that only a contract closes them.
- **Contracts state the value:** `assert:` can now say what the call returns (`0 <= result && result < bound`). Such contracts are tested on a real JVM like the others, and a refuted one says what the JVM actually returned: "on i=0 the JVM's call returns 32".

**Two behaviours changed:**
- **Unreplayable witness:** a counterexample that goes through a contract, and that the interpreter can't run, is now "no verdict" instead of a violation. A contract allows values the real call may never give. This turns one 3b test result (`firstByte`) from a violation into no verdict.

Contracts for gaps can now be **proved** against the JDK's own bytecode. That's the strongest of the three evidence levels, above tested and trusted. It's committed as `usrpuywy`, and the commit check reported 0 errors.

**How it works:**
- **Which contracts:** those for a static JDK method whose parameters are all primitives, such as `Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros`. Before the JVM test runs, the tool's own checker runs that method's real bytecode, copied from the JDK image, on every input the contract covers.
- **What it checks:** the same things the JVM test does, with the exception class having to match exactly. A small new engine function compares the classes.
- **When a contract counts as proved:** only if the proof holds and the JVM test doesn't refute it either. The result records the class, the JDK version, the class file's hash and the proof's size.
- **When a proof finds a counterexample:** that input is added to the JVM test, so a contract is only refuted by what a real JVM does. If the JVM disagrees with the proof, the contract stays at tested and the disagreement is recorded. Every contract that isn't proved records why.

**What the tests show:**
- `numberOfLeadingZeros`'s contract is now proved, where before it was only tested.
- A contract that is wrong only at `i = 777777` used to pass as tested, because no test input reaches that value. Now the proof finds it and the JVM confirms it.
